reference.source: WHO Classification of Female Genital Tumours
clinicalPearls: A malignant germ-cell tumour, distinguished from the common mature cystic teratoma by the presence of immature, embryonal-type tissue
Occurs chiefly in children and young women and often presents as a rapidly enlarging, predominantly solid pelvic mass
The grade is determined by the amount of immature neuroepithelium present, and grade strongly influences behaviour and treatment
Alpha-fetoprotein may be mildly elevated, and a significant rise should prompt a search for a coexisting yolk sac component
Peritoneal implants of mature glial tissue (gliomatosis peritonei) can accompany the tumour and, when purely mature, do not themselves indicate malignancy
Typically unilateral, allowing fertility-sparing surgery in many young patients
Chemosensitive, so platinum-based germ-cell chemotherapy is used for higher-grade or advanced disease
reference.pathophysiology: Immature teratomas are germ-cell tumours containing tissues from all three embryonic layers, but unlike mature teratomas they include immature, embryonal-appearing elements, most importantly primitive neuroepithelium forming rosettes and tubules. The quantity of this immature neuroepithelium underlies the histological grading system, with higher grades reflecting greater immaturity and more aggressive potential. Because the tumour arises from a germ cell, it may coexist with other germ-cell elements, and any yolk sac component can raise serum alpha-fetoprotein. Mature glial implants on the peritoneum (gliomatosis peritonei) represent differentiation of tumour tissue and, when entirely mature, carry a benign course, whereas immature implants indicate genuine dissemination.
additionalDifferentials: Other malignant germ-cell tumours (yolk sac tumour, dysgerminoma, embryonal carcinoma)
additionalInvestigations: Serum AFP, beta-hCG, and LDH to assess for mixed germ-cell components
Transabdominal and transvaginal ultrasound of a solid or mixed ovarian mass
Cross-sectional imaging (CT or MRI) for staging and detection of peritoneal implants
Histology with grading of immature neuroepithelium
Assessment of any peritoneal deposits to distinguish mature from immature implants
redFlags: A rapidly enlarging, predominantly solid ovarian mass in a child or young woman
Rising alpha-fetoprotein indicating a possible yolk sac component
Immature peritoneal implants signifying true metastatic spread
reference.prognosis: Depends heavily on grade and stage; low-grade, early-stage tumours have an excellent outlook, and higher-grade or advanced disease responds well to chemotherapy so that cure remains common, often with fertility preserved.
pitfalls: Failing to distinguish an immature (malignant) teratoma from a benign mature cystic teratoma
Not grading the neuroepithelial component, which guides adjuvant treatment
Misinterpreting mature gliomatosis peritonei as malignant dissemination
Overlooking a yolk sac component signalled by a rising AFP
references: WHO Classification of Female Genital Tumours
Blaustein's Pathology of the Female Genital Tract
management: Start with surgical staging (peritoneal washing, inspection and biopsy of peritoneal surfaces, omental and nodal assessment) for any suspected malignant ovarian germ cell tumour.

Prefer fertility-sparing unilateral salpingo-oophorectomy plus staging over bilateral resection or hysterectomy, since these tumours are almost always unilateral and highly chemosensitive; this can be considered even when metastases are present.
For FIGO stage IA, grade 1 or 2 immature teratoma, surgery alone (fertility-sparing resection plus staging) is a reasonable approach without adjuvant chemotherapy.

For higher grade or higher stage disease, give adjuvant combination chemotherapy built on a platinum agent with etoposide and bleomycin, following the treatment experience extrapolated from testicular germ cell cancer.
There is no established role for radiotherapy in immature teratoma of the ovary, unlike the radiosensitive dysgerminoma.
When assessing extra-ovarian disease, distinguish purely mature peritoneal implants (gliomatosis peritonei) from immature implants, and reserve additional treatment for immature deposits.
For relapsed or refractory disease, consider salvage chemotherapy using principles extrapolated from testicular germ cell cancer, along with surgical resection of residual masses.
Follow alpha-fetoprotein and human chorionic gonadotropin serially to help detect a mixed germ cell component and to track disease activity, though no specific surveillance interval is defined.
Monitor for return of menstrual function and fertility outcomes, since return of normal menses is the rule and successful pregnancies are well documented in survivors of this tumour group.
Arrange longer-term surveillance imaging with a defined follow-up schedule as part of routine post-treatment care.

Manage patients within a gynaecological oncology multidisciplinary team with fertility-preservation counselling before any treatment decision, given the rarity of this tumour, the extrapolated evidence base, and the typically young patient population.
Refer back to gynaecological oncology for reassessment and consideration of further surgery if tumour markers rise after treatment or if growing teratoma syndrome is suspected.
Overall prognosis for this class of ovarian germ cell malignancy is excellent.
